title: Tenali and the Arabian Horse

full_text:
An Arabian sea-captain docked at the port of Bhatkal and brought to Vijayanagara an exquisite, pure-bred Arabian stallion named Buraq. The horse was graceful, with high-arched neck, slender limbs, and eyes like liquid fire. The captain asked four thousand gold dinars for the stallion.

Envious courtiers who had not received bribes from the sea-captain whispered poison into King Krishnadevaraya's ear:
'Maharaj, be not deceived! This horse has a secret defect: its left hind leg is weak, and it is blind in night travel. It is unfit for imperial cavalry.'

The King, hesitant to spend royal funds on a flawed beast, was about to reject the captain when Tenali Raman spoke:
'Maharaj, words of praise and words of slander are equally cheap. A warhorse is not tested by the whispers of courtiers standing safely on velvet carpets, but by the road itself. Let me test this stallion tonight on the Obstacle Course of the Seven Terraces!'

The courtiers smirked, expecting Tenali to fall and break his bones.
At midnight, under a moonless, overcast sky, Tenali arrived at the testing grounds.
He did not use a whip or spurs. He blindfolded his own eyes with a black silk scarf, mounted the Arabian stallion, and loosened the reins completely!

'Ride, Buraq!' cried Tenali.
The stallion surged forward into the pitch-black course!
Navigating winding ditches, wooden hurdles, sharp turns, and narrow stone bridges, the noble horse leaped over obstacles with breathtaking instinct, guided purely by its own extraordinary night vision and equine intelligence!
It completed the entire treacherous circuit without tripping a single peg or stumbling once, returning to the royal pavilion in flawless stride!

Tenali removed his blindfold and dismounted gracefully:
'Behold, Your Majesty! A horse that can carry a blindfolded rider through a labyrinth in the dark without a scratch has neither weak limbs nor defective sight! The only blindness present was in the envious eyes of those who sought to disparage true excellence!'

King Krishnadevaraya was overjoyed. He purchased the stallion immediately, rewarded the honest Arab captain, and punished the slanderers, while Tenali showed that genuine virtue shines brightest when put to the test.
moral: Envy attempts to discredit genuine excellence; practical testing under impartial conditions vindicates quality.
